world_behind.title: The classroom convenes
world_behind.text: For once the brothers come to Nephi with a question instead of a rod: "What meaneth these things which ye have read" (v. 1), framed in the era's live debate about prophecy: "according to the spirit and not the flesh" (v. 1) Their instinct to file Isaiah under "spiritual only" is the safe reading; safe readings ask nothing of the reader.

world_behind.title: The tribes already gone
world_behind.text: "The more part of all the tribes have been led away" (v. 4) states sober history: Assyria emptied the northern kingdom more than a century before Lehi left, and where those deportees went was unknown in Jerusalem then and after. The record's "whither they are none of us knoweth" (v. 4) is honest agnosticism, rare in any era's prophecy talk.

world_behind.title: A mighty nation, located
world_behind.text: Nephi reads Isaiah's nursing Gentiles as future history with an address: "a mighty nation among the Gentiles, yea, even upon the face of this land" (v. 7). The interpretation plants the fulfillment on his own hemisphere. The record's long interest in what the Gentiles of this land eventually do with it starts here.

world_behind.title: Malachi before Malachi
world_behind.text: The stubble that burns (v. 15) and the "calves of the stall" (v. 24) run word for word with Malachi 4:1–2, written well after Lehi's departure. Either the brass plates carried the older prophetic stock Malachi drew on, or the same Lord speaks the same sentences twice; the record, which later has Christ deliver Malachi entire (3 Ne. 24–25), never feels the difficulty it leaves us.

world_behind.title: A binding without chains
world_behind.text: Revelation chains the dragon for a thousand years; Nephi's mechanics are different: "because of the righteousness of his people, Satan has no power" (v. 26). The binding is demand-side: hearts in righteousness leave the tempter unemployed. Same millennium, but this record locates the padlock in the people.

world_behind.title: The editor's restraint
world_behind.text: "I durst not speak further as yet concerning these things" (v. 29): the same boundary drawn in the vision chapters (the sealed portions of ch. 14) governs the teacher's mouth. The small plates end their first book because the permission ran out, with material still in hand.

words.text: Scattered "and be confounded" (v. 5): mixed past recognition, identity dissolved among the nations. Treated at 1 Nephi 14:2. The word is the scattering's real damage, the loss of the name itself. The promise runs the other way in the same vocabulary: the righteous "are those who shall not be confounded" (v. 22).

words.text: Gathered Israel comes "out of obscurity and out of darkness" (v. 12): out of unnoticedness as well as captivity. Obscurity is the condition of the confounded, existing without being identified; the gathering's first gift is being known again, by the Lord and by themselves.

words.text: To fall over, and in this record always of something built or standing coming down. It appears seven times here and never in the King James Bible. Its first use is the destruction at the crucifixion, where mountains tumble into pieces and cities tumble to the earth (1 Ne. 12:4). Here it takes the great and abominable church, which "shall tumble to the dust and great shall be the fall of it" (v. 14). The verb makes the collapse ordinary, the way a stacked thing gives way.

words.text: Not a King James word at all. The translation steps outside that vocabulary three times in the volume, and all three describe religion arranged for applause: Nehor teaching that priests "ought to become popular" (Alma 1:3), the popular part of the Zoramites refusing Alma because his preaching hurt their craft (Alma 35:3), and here churches "built up to become popular in the eyes of the world" (v. 23). The measuring instrument gets named in the same breath, other people's eyes, which is what marks this build off from the two beside it.

The record refuses the either/or its questioners offer; prophecy manifests by the Spirit and arrives "according to the flesh" (v. 2).

Isaiah's favorite divine title becomes the interpretation's spine, and its climactic claim: Moses' prophet "was the Holy One of Israel" (v. 21).

phrases.text: The interpretation's boldest concrete prediction: a specific Gentile power "upon the face of this land" (v. 7), instrument of both scattering ("by them shall our seed be scattered" (v. 7)) and nursing (v. 8). The record holds both without contradiction: the same nation is rod and cradle, depending on the decade.

In chapter 14 it was set before the Gentiles as a choice; here it is the engine of the whole gathering, and the record itself is the work's advance copy.

phrases.term: Saved, even if it so be as by fire
phrases.text: The preservation formula: "he will preserve the righteous by his power" (v. 17), even when the deliverance route runs through the flame that takes everything else. Paul will build the same figure (1 Cor. 3:15). Safety in this chapter is never exemption from the fire; it is ownership of what survives it.

verses.label: v. 1
verses.title: The chapter opens on a question about method
verses.text: What the brothers ask is not what happens next but how the text is to be taken: "are they to be understood according to things which are spiritual, which shall come to pass according to the spirit and not the flesh?" The record gives them a technical question and a defensible one, which is not how it usually presents them; at 1 Nephi 15:8–9 the same brothers are shown declining to inquire at all. Everything after verse 2 is answer, so the chapter is structured as commentary and its occasion is stated in its first sentence.

verses.label: v. 6–8
verses.title: One borrowed clause used three times in two chapters
verses.text: The record draws the image of children carried in arms and on shoulders straight from the block just quoted, at 1 Nephi 21:22, "they shall bring thy sons in their arms, and thy daughters shall be carried upon their shoulders." Verse 6 restates it as accomplished, "their children have been carried in their arms, and their daughters have been carried upon their shoulders," and verse 8 compresses it to "being carried in their arms and upon their shoulders." Three appearances, three different tenses and lengths. The middle one carries the interpretive verdict attached to it: "behold these things of which are spoken are temporal."

verses.label: v. 9
verses.title: The covenant supplied in its oldest wording
verses.text: The exposition reaches past Isaiah to quote Abraham's promise directly: "In thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed." The wording tracks Genesis 22:18 and 26:4 with "kindreds" where the King James text has "nations," a substitution the record makes consistently, as at 1 Nephi 15:18 and 3 Nephi 20:25. The chapter thus rests a reading of Isaiah on a text older than Isaiah, and names the source as the Father's covenant with Abraham rather than as a book.

verses.label: v. 15–17
verses.title: A prophet quoted three times and never named
verses.text: The record attributes twice by title alone, "saith the prophet" at verse 15 and "thus saith the prophet" at verse 17, then a third time at verse 23, "according to the words of the prophet." The imagery in all three is Malachi's: the proud and the wicked as stubble, the burning day, and at verse 24 "calves of the stall," which is Malachi 4:1–2. The record has this material available and quotes it at length under Malachi's name in 3 Nephi 24 and 25, so the anonymity here is a feature of this chapter and not of the whole record.

verses.label: v. 20
verses.title: The one source the chapter does name
verses.text: Moses is named and quoted: "A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you, like unto me; him shall ye hear in all things whatsoever he shall say unto you." The wording follows Deuteronomy 18:15 and 18:18–19, with the two verses of that passage joined into one sentence and the warning of verse 19 folded in after it. In a chapter that leaves Isaiah and Malachi unnamed, the single attribution by name goes to the lawgiver, and verse 21 immediately supplies an identification the source does not make.

verses.label: v. 22–23
verses.title: The same verb assigned to both groups
verses.text: Verse 22 says the righteous "need not fear"; verse 23 says the members of the devil's kingdom "are they who need fear, and tremble, and quake." The record sets the two clauses a verse apart and lets the repetition do the sorting. Verse 23 then defines the second group by four purposes rather than by doctrine: built up to get gain, to get power over the flesh, to become popular in the eyes of the world, and to seek the lusts of the flesh. Three of the four concern standing among people, and none of them concerns belief.

verses.label: v. 29
verses.title: A stated limit on the record
verses.text: The chapter stops on a refusal, not a conclusion: "I durst not speak further as yet concerning these things." The record marks the boundary rather than passing over it silently, which is a habit that recurs at 1 Nephi 14:28 and 3 Nephi 26:11. Two verses of practical instruction follow, on the plates of brass being true and on obedience, so what is withheld is the visionary material and what is kept is the part the brothers can act on.

chapter.title: The discussion the reading was for
chapter.text: Two chapters of Isaiah end in a question-and-answer session, as the unit's design required: purpose (19), text (20–21), interpretation (22). The brothers ask Nephi rather than the Lord, as in chapter 15, but they ask, and the record rewards the question with its longest answer yet.

chapter.title: Temporal and spiritual, permanently
chapter.text: The question at verse 1 offers one option, "are they to be understood according to things which are spiritual," and the answer at verse 3 refuses to take it, "things pertaining to things both temporal and spiritual." Verse 6 then labels a specific passage, "behold these things of which are spoken are temporal," and verse 27 closes with "all these things must come according to the flesh." The rule is stated three times in one chapter, and 2 Nephi 25:1–5 gives the same distinction as the reason Isaiah is hard for these hearers.

chapter.title: The covenant arc, stated once, entire
chapter.text: Scattering for hardening; a Gentile nation as rod and then cradle; a marvelous work; the bared arm; gathering out of obscurity. This is the whole record's plot, laid out at the first book's close like an overture, and everything after it is enactment.

chapter.title: Judgment is self-service
chapter.text: Blood on their own heads, drunk on their own blood, swords of their own hands, the pit of their own digging: the chapter's destruction verbs are all reflexive. God's stated role is on the other ledger, preserving the righteous; the wicked are given only what they built.

chapter.title: Fear is assigned
chapter.text: "The righteous need not fear" twice, and one class that must: the catalogue of verse 23. The chapter treats fear as a fact about allegiance, which converts anxiety about the last days into a diagnostic question about the present ones.

chapter.title: The boldest identification
chapter.text: Pinning Deuteronomy's prophet-like-Moses on the Holy One of Israel is the interpretation's peak claim, the same one Peter will preach on the temple steps (Acts 3:22). The record's christology is not an addendum to the covenant story; it is the covenant story's subject.

chapter.title: A book ends on plainness
chapter.text: First Nephi closes with obedience and endurance, the two least glamorous words in its vocabulary. The sign-off "And thus it is. Amen." seals a book whose argument has been, from the first verse's goodly parents, that the record is true and that truth asks something.

applications.title: Ask the meaning question
applications.text: The brothers' one great hour in this book begins with "What meaneth these things?" After your next reading, ask it out loud of one passage, and refuse the safe spiritual-only answer until you have also asked what it predicts, requires, or changes in the flesh.

applications.title: Read one prophecy as addressed mail
applications.text: Take a gathering or covenant promise and apply Nephi's "it meaneth us": write down what it means for your family line, your generation, your ward. Likening ends where "us" begins.

applications.title: Join the marvelous work at hand level
applications.text: The work of great worth runs on carried children and nursing strangers. Pick one concrete task this month (family history, a convert's first weeks, a returning member's dinner table) and be logistics for the gathering.

applications.title: Run the verse 23 audit
applications.text: Gain, power over others, popularity, appetite: test your institutions and your own projects against the four builds. Anything that fails the audit belongs, by the chapter's own list, to a kingdom with a short lease.

applications.title: Retire an assigned fear
applications.text: List what the last days currently cost you in dread, then read the refrain: the righteous need not fear. Move the energy from forecasting to allegiance; the chapter locates safety in whose you are.

applications.title: Bind Satan at household scale
applications.text: The millennium's mechanism, righteousness leaving the tempter powerless, does not wait for the millennium. Choose the one recurring temptation in your home and starve it structurally this week: no power because no purchase.

questions.text: When I ask what scripture means, am I hoping the answer stays spiritual, and what would a temporal answer require of me?
What part of my own family is currently "led away, and none of us knoweth whither," and what does this chapter promise about them?
Where in my life am I trusting that evil will simply fall into its own pit, and where am I called to do more than wait?
Which fire am I asking to be exempted from that God has only promised to bring me through?
Of the four builds (gain, power, popularity, appetite), which one funds my most respectable ambitions?
If my record ended today with one closing sentence, what would it testify that a man must do?
